title: Delhi, 1783
hook: Baghel Singh camped at Delhi and marked the sites where gurdwaras like Sis Ganj now stand

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lahore, and coins struck in the Gurus' names: deg, teg, fateh. Your line was the gurus' coin. Who did you give credit to? Today, the Khalsa reaches the capital. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

A Sikh army is camped outside Delhi, the seat of the Mughal emperors. The court is nervous. The army's leader, Baghel Singh, could ask for a great deal: money, land, a share of the city's wealth. The court wants him gone. Tradition says that along with a share of the city's taxes, he asked for something stranger: to stay a while, and to find and mark the places in the city where the Gurus had been. Today: Delhi.
screen: `A SIKH ARMY OUTSIDE DELHI.` → `THE COURT WANTS HIM GONE.` → `HE ASKS FOR THE GURUS' PLACES.`

segments.voice: Start with why Delhi mattered. Guru Tegh Bahadur was put to death in Delhi, in the middle of the city; Sikhs remember it as the price of standing up for other people's freedom to worship. Sikhs knew roughly where. But the city had moved on. Shops, houses and other buildings stood on ground Sikhs remembered as sacred. Second, what Baghel Singh did. Tradition says he set about finding the exact spots: where the Guru was beheaded, where his body was secretly cremated, where other Gurus had stayed. Some of it, tradition says, came down to asking people who remembered. Then the places were marked, so that gurdwaras could rise there. Third, the name you can still find on a map of Delhi: Sis Ganj. Sis is an old word for head, still used in Punjabi. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib stands in Chandni Chowk, a crowded old market street, on the place Sikhs remember as where the Guru gave his head. There's a deeper day on this path later for the Guru's death itself. Today's story is the marking. Fourth, the point for an ordinary life. Armies come and go, and their camps are forgotten. The gurdwaras he marked still draw people in today. He used his one moment of power to make sure a memory had a place to live. Marking the places.
screen: `THE GURU WAS KILLED IN DELHI.` · `FINDING THE EXACT SPOTS.` · `SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.` · `A MEMORY GIVEN A PLACE TO LIVE.` · then, large: `MARKING THE PLACES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in a gurdwara. If there's one near you, you can go in any day; anyone is welcome, with head covered and shoes off. If not, picture one. The steps worn smooth. Shoes left at the door. A cloth over your hair. Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib under its canopy, and someone singing. Sit at the back, in your mind or for real, and breathe. Notice that this room stands on a spot someone chose to remember. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Delhi. Tradition says Baghel Singh, camped at the capital, found and marked the places where the Gurus had been, so that gurdwaras like Sis Ganj could stand there. Today's word.
Your line: marking the places. Today, pass a place where something mattered to you, or to someone you love, and stop there for one breath. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, is visited by Sikhs and others; Baghel Singh's role in marking Delhi's Sikh sites is told in Sikh histories.

Sites named generally: where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded (Sis Ganj), where his body was cremated (Rakab Ganj), where other Gurus stayed (e.g. Bangla Sahib, Majnu ka Tilla); confirm.
'Some of it came down to asking people who remembered' is offered as 'tradition says'; the common telling involves local testimony about the Sis Ganj site; confirm or cut.
